name: Jade Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run bagging machines at a frozen vegetable plant, the one by the canal that does peas, sweetcorn and mixed veg for supermarket own brands. The bagger takes the frozen veg from the hopper, weighs it, fills the bag and seals it, and then it goes over the checkweigher, which is a scale that kicks out any bag that's under or over. I'm in charge of three lines of that, changing the film rolls, sorting out jams and keeping the weights right. The packing hall is kept at four degrees, so I wear two fleeces in July.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a busy day look like, compared with a quiet one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In pea season, June and July, it's twelve-hour days and the trucks come in straight from the fields, so you can't stop. In winter it's slower and they cut our hours, which is the hard part with money. I use one of those AI apps sometimes, for meal plans when we're skint or to check Ellie's maths homework, but at work I don't need it. My lunch is usually with Precious from quality, we sit in the van because it's warmer than the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that was a lot of headlines for not much. I'd probably share a funny meme about it in the family group. That's about as online as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays the same, which is good. The money stays tight, which isn't. But I'd rather have tight and steady than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. I'd try to save a bit from pea season to cover the winter hours cut, which we never quite manage. Maybe I'd use the app more to plan the shopping, it's handy for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. That's how life feels anyway, same as last year, same as next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned winter hours being cut. What happened last winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter I got a quarter less pay for three months. Dan, my partner, does deliveries for a parcel firm, so we leaned on his overtime at Christmas. We got through, but we used the credit card more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what would you want to keep exactly as it is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pea season, honestly. People think it's hard, and it is, but everyone pulls together and there's a buzz, and the money's good. I'd keep that.

S0.say: That was a lot of headlines for not much. She'd share a funny meme in the family group, which is about as online as she gets.
S0.think: The job stays the same, which is good, and money stays tight, which isn't. She'd rather have tight and steady than nothing.
S0.do: Keeps working as before and tries to save part of her pea-season pay to cover the winter hours cut. Uses the AI app more to plan the shopping.
S0.feel: Calm, because that's how life already feels, the same from year to year.
S0.quote: I'd rather have tight and steady than nothing.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is practical and unflustered in the plateau picture. Her real money pressure is seasonal: winter hours cuts that push the family onto the credit card. She speaks warmly about the shared effort of pea season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it makes sense, the baggers already practically run themselves. The company needs to be clear with us about what's changing and when. People handle change better when they're told early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about both of us, not just me. Dan's job is driving and that's one they talk about robots doing too. If my lines get merged and his routes shrink in the same couple of years, we're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the first new line looks like, then put my name down to be trained as a line technician, that's one up from me. We'd stop the credit card and cut the streaming and the kids' after-school club to one day. And I'd ask Dan to look into what his firm's plans are, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it'd be on my mind every time a manager walked through with someone in a suit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait to see the first line, rather than putting your name down now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen new kit come in before, and the first version is always a mess. Last time they put in a new film sealer it broke every week for six months. I'd let it settle, then go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dan do if both of you were squeezed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to be honest with each other. I'd sit down with Dan on a Sunday night and do the numbers properly, which we usually avoid.

S1.say: Some of it makes sense, since the baggers already practically run themselves. The company should tell workers clearly and early what's changing.
S1.think: She's worried about the whole household, because her partner drives for a parcel firm and that's also in line for robots. Both jobs shrinking at once would put them in trouble.
S1.do: Waits to see the first new line settle, then asks to train as a line technician. Stops using the credit card, cuts streaming and the after-school club to one day, and asks her partner to find out his firm's plans quietly.
S1.feel: Anxious but not panicking, on edge whenever a manager walks through with someone in a suit.
S1.quote: If my lines get merged and his routes shrink in the same couple of years, we're in trouble.
S1.fieldNote: Jade's worry is about two exposed jobs in one household rather than her own alone. Her wait for new kit to settle is based on direct experience with a faulty sealer. She plans to face the household numbers she usually avoids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in fast, with money for families, and the companies need to give proper notice. I'm not one for marches, but I'd sign anything going round. And I'd say it's madness to let it happen this quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would knock both of us out at once. The plant and the parcel firm would both be first in the queue for robots. Two years isn't enough to do anything clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd write down every bill and cut what we can, the car Dan uses for himself would go. I'd look for anything less likely to go robot quickly, maybe a care home or a school kitchen, even for less money. We'd talk to my mum about moving in with her if we couldn't keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A care home job, when robots could reach hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it's not a long-term answer. But in a two-year rush I think they'd go for the factories and warehouses first and the care homes later, because it's harder there. Later is all I'm asking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellie's twelve, she'd notice. I'd tell her we're tightening our belts and it's not her fault, and I'd keep Max's football going as long as I could. It's the one thing he lives for.

S2.say: The government needs to step in fast with money for families, and companies need to give proper notice. She's not one for marches but would sign anything going round.
S2.think: It would knock out both her and her partner's jobs at once, since the plant and the parcel firm would be first for robots. Two years isn't enough to do anything clever.
S2.do: Lists every bill in the first month and sells her partner's car. Looks for work less likely to automate quickly, like a care home or school kitchen, even for less money, and talks to her mother about moving in if they lose the house.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd keep Max's football going as long as I could. It's the one thing he lives for.
S2.fieldNote: Jade's response stays orderly even under pressure: a list of bills, a fallback job and a family safety net. She's honest that the care home move only buys time. Protecting her son's football is where her feelings show most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if people start now. I'd tell everyone at work to get a certificate in something while the company's still paying for training. That's my practical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years would let me watch the first plants go robot and learn from them. I'd still lose the job, I think, but I'd have a chance to be ready. And Ellie would be seventeen, nearly out of school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the line technician course in the first year, because it's free through work. I'd try to save something every month from Dan's overtime. And we'd sit down with Ellie about what she wants to study, and make sure it's something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. Like having a plan for the winter hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a certificate, if AGI is coming anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a certificate is portable, it goes with you. Even if the technician jobs only last a few years, they'd last longer than the bagging jobs. You buy time where you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before you were pushed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd be ready to go before they push me. If I saw the robots coming I'd rather look for a job while I've still got one.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if people start now. She'd tell colleagues to get a certificate in something while the company still pays for training.
S3.think: Five years would let her watch the first plants automate and learn from them. She'd likely still lose the job but have a chance to be ready, with her daughter nearly out of school.
S3.do: Takes the free line technician course through work in the first year and saves from her partner's overtime each month. Talks with her daughter about studying something that involves people.
S3.feel: Anxious, but more in control, like having a plan for winter hours.
S3.quote: A certificate is portable, it goes with you.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Jade's steady style into a plan she trusts: watch others, take the free course, leave before being pushed. She openly treats training as a way of buying time rather than a lasting fix. Her daughter's study choice becomes part of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if anyone's sensible about it. Companies, government and families can all plan. I'd say it in that calm way that annoys people who want an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still ends with no job, but ten years is a lifetime in my house. The kids would be grown, the mortgage much smaller. I think we'd come out of it smaller but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the others but slower. Technician course after a couple of years, once I'd seen it work, and look at a move to a job with people in it in my late forties. Pay something extra off the mortgage every pea season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I'd have time to get used to the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools more, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd use AI tools a bit more. You'd be daft not to learn how they work if they're going to be everywhere. I'd do what I do now, pick it up once Dan's brother has tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen first in your house, in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan's firm, probably. Robots driving vans might come before robots running a frozen pea line. Then it'd be on me to carry us for a while.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time if anyone's sensible, and companies, government and families can all plan. She'd say it in the calm way that annoys people who want an argument.
S4.think: It still ends with no job, but ten years is a lifetime in her house: children grown and the mortgage much smaller. She thinks they'd come out of it smaller but okay.
S4.do: Takes the technician course after a couple of years, once it's proven, and plans a move to people-focused work in her late forties. Pays extra off the mortgage every pea season and gradually uses AI tools more.
S4.feel: Anxious but steady, with time to get used to the idea.
S4.quote: I'd say it in that calm way that annoys people who want an argument.
S4.fieldNote: Jade's plan is the same as in five years but stretched out, and she knows she'd only pick up AI once a relative has tried it. Her worry shifts to her partner's job going first. The end point still bothers her, but the decade gives the family time to shrink safely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits me and Dan at once. What would help is a proper bridge: some money for families while they retrain, and companies made to give a year's notice. Something you can plan around.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the winter. Everyone talks about robots and jobs, but in our place the hours go up and down with the harvest already. Any plan has to cope with people like us who never had steady hours to begin with.

headlineQuote: Any plan has to cope with people like us who never had steady hours to begin with.
portrait: Jade Wagner, 43, runs three bagging lines in the cold packing hall of a frozen vegetable plant, with a partner, Dan, who drives for a parcel firm, two children and pay that drops every winter. She uses AI now and then for meal plans and homework, and likes to let new things prove themselves before she commits. She is calm in the plateau, but steady change already makes her anxious because both her job and Dan's are exposed. Two-year AGI alarms her and she reaches for an orderly survival plan; five and ten years let her map out courses and a move to people-focused work. Her tone stays level throughout, and she judges every option by whether it buys time.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would hit her job and her partner's at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A proper bridge of money for families while they retrain, and companies required to give a year's notice.
